hops.title: How a smell really crosses a room
hops.text: Spray perfume in one corner, and someone across the room smells it within seconds. Diffusion usually gets the credit, but it is too slow for that trip. In still air, diffusion alone could take about a day to spread some perfume ingredients a meter. Moving air does most of the carrying. Diffusion helps spread the scent too, and it crosses the last tiny gap at the lining of the nose.

sources.citation: MathBench Biology Modules, Diffusion: A fragrant example. University of Maryland.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: water crosses a choosy membrane
hops.title: Why seawater makes a thirsty person thirstier
hops.text: Lost at sea, a person has water everywhere and none to drink. Human kidneys cannot make urine as salty as seawater. So clearing the salt from a drink takes more water than the drink provided. Drink enough, and the blood gets saltier than the liquid inside the body's cells. Cell membranes hold most of that salt back, so water drifts out, the same way it leaves a salted cucumber.

hops.title: Soak raisins and compare them with a dry one
hops.text: A raisin is a dried grape packed with sugar. Its skin lets water through. Put a few in a clear glass of plain water and keep one dry beside it. After a day, compare a soaked raisin with the dry one. What difference do you see? Which way did the water move, and what did the sugar have to do with it? Throw the soaked ones away without tasting them.
